core: The working definition of debit and credit, attributed: debit is the left side of an account or journal entry, credit is the right side (OpenStax Principles of Accounting, Section 3.5; CFI Debit Credit Analysis)
Debit and credit carry no inherent good or bad meaning; each side increases some account types and decreases others
The rules named, one line per account type: assets and expenses increase with debits; liabilities, equity, and revenue increase with credits
Why the rules exist: every entry records equal debits and credits, which keeps the accounting equation balanced (the equation is a sibling topic, referenced only)
T-accounts: the simple two-column picture of an account, debit side left and credit side right, used when posting journal information to the ledger
Debit and credit in action with an original example: buying supplies with cash is a debit to Supplies and a credit to Cash, with the mechanics shown
The common confusion: debit does not mean bad and credit does not mean good
The honest framing: learn the five one-line rules once and the whole system follows
supporting: The journal as the book of original entry — the first place transaction information enters the accounting system (OpenStax Section 3.5)
The double-entry shape of a transaction: at least one debit and one credit, with equal total amounts (CFI Debit Credit Analysis; OpenStax Section 3.5 simple vs compound entries)
The classical real/personal/nominal account framework as an older teaching tradition that reaches the same debits-and-credits outcomes (CFI Debit Credit Analysis)
The equation as the reason the convention exists: assets = liabilities + equity, and balanced entries keep it in balance (OpenStax Section 3.5; CFI Accounting Equation; OpenStax Section 3.2)
outOfScope: How journal entries are formatted, dated, and ordered (sibling topic: accounting:foundations:journal-entries; referenced only)
The accounting equation's full mechanics and expanded form (sibling topic: accounting:foundations:accounting-equation; referenced only)
The general ledger, account numbering, and running balances (sibling topic: accounting:foundations:general-ledger; referenced only)
The trial balance and what it checks (sibling topic: accounting:foundations:trial-balance; referenced only)
Assets, liabilities, equity, revenue, and expenses as concepts (sibling topics: assets, liabilities, equity, revenue, expenses; referenced only)

claims.claim: A journal entry has debit and credit columns: the debit is on the left side and the credit is on the right side — the working definition of the two terms used in this lesson, attributed to OpenStax's Principles of Accounting and stated identically by CFI.
Debit and credit are names for positions, not judgments: each side increases some account types and decreases others, so neither word carries an inherent good or bad meaning.
Assets increase on the debit side and decrease on the credit side.
Expenses increase on the debit side: OpenStax records utility and salaries expenses as debits, and CFI's rule is to debit the expense account when its balance increases.
Liabilities increase on the credit side and decrease on the debit side: OpenStax shows Accounts Payable increasing with a credit.
Equity and revenue increase on the credit side: OpenStax credits Common Stock (equity) when stock is issued for cash and credits Service Revenue when services are provided.

Every transaction is recorded with at least one debit and one credit, and the total dollar amounts in the debit and credit columns must always be equal for the entry to balance — the double-entry rule.

The debit-credit rules exist so the accounting equation stays balanced: once journal entries are posted to T-accounts, the business checks that the accounting equation remains balanced, and CFI states that the debit and credit transactions balance the equation.
A T-account is the two-column picture of an account — debit side on the left, credit side on the right — used when posting journal information to the ledger.

Buying supplies is recorded with a debit to Supplies (an asset, which increases with debits), and paying with cash is recorded with a credit to Cash (an asset, which decreases with credits) — the mechanics shown in this lesson's original supplies-for-cash example.
The journal is the first place information enters the accounting system, often called the book of original entry.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Two teaching frameworks explain which side to use: the modern balance-sheet approach by account type versus the classical real/personal/nominal approach.
positions: Modern approach (OpenStax; CFI's balance-sheet section): assets and expenses increase with debits; liabilities, equity, and revenue increase with credits

Classical approach (CFI's 'classical approach' section): real accounts debit what comes in and credit what goes out; personal accounts debit the receiver and credit the giver; nominal accounts debit expense and loss and credit income and profit
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the modern by-account-type rules used in financial accounting courses and by OpenStax, and notes the classical framework only as an older tradition reaching the same outcomes; the two frameworks are not treated as conflicting in the lesson itself.

conflictingEvidence.issue: CFI's one-line rule mentions 'liability/income account' while OpenStax treats equity and revenue as separate credit-side types.
positions: CFI: 'debit the asset/expense account and credit the liability/income account'
OpenStax Section 3.5: assets and expenses increase on the debit side; liabilities, equity (Common Stock), and revenue (Service Revenue) increase on the credit side
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names the five account types separately — assets and expenses with debits; liabilities, equity, and revenue with credits — which is the more complete statement and consistent with both sources; CFI's compressed version is quoted as corroboration.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Accounting, Volume 1: Financial Accounting, Section 3.5: Use Journal Entries to Record Transactions and Post to T-Accounts
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Read live via curl from openstax.org on 2026-08-21 (page footer confirms the book may not be used to train or be ingested into LLMs without OpenStax's permission; respected). Supports: the journal as the first place information enters the accounting system (book of original entry); the journal's debit (left) and credit (right) columns; the one-line rules by account type — assets increase on the debit side and decrease on the credit side, a liability account such as Accounts Payable increases on the credit side and decreases on the debit side; worked entries showing Common Stock (equity) credited when stock is issued for cash, Service Revenue credited when services are provided, Utility Expense and Salaries Expense debited when paid, and Supplies debited when purchased; the T-account format used when posting journal information to the ledger; the check that the accounting equation remains balanced once entries are posted; simple (one debit, one credit) versus compound entries. Facts restated in original prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Debit Credit Analysis
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B (reputable secondary). Read live via curl on 2026-08-21. Supports: debit on the left side and credit on the right side of an account; debit and credit as the backbone of the double-entry system, with every transaction comprising two parts — for every debit, a corresponding credit of an equal amount; the total dollar amounts in the debit and credit columns must always be equal for the entry to balance; the one-line rule that increasing balances debit the asset/expense account and credit the liability/income account; balance-sheet effects (a debit increases the asset side, a credit reduces it; on the liability side a debit decreases and a credit increases, with a loan credited to long-term debt and debited to cash balancing the equation); a $10,000 equipment purchase by check debiting equipment and crediting cash; a $10,000 salary payment crediting cash and debiting salary expense; the classical real/personal/nominal account framework as an older teaching tradition. Facts synthesized into original prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Accounting Equation
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B, reused from content/phase-2/source-registry.json (identical id and URL). Supports: the equation assets = liabilities + shareholders' equity as the foundation of double-entry accounting and the mechanism by which an increase in an asset is matched by an equal increase in a liability or equity account (or an equal decrease in another asset) so the equation stays in balance — cited in this lesson for why the debit-credit rules exist.
